message.content:
In Texas, tenants have several statutory protections and responsibilities under the Texas Property Code and related laws. Here’s a quick overview of your key rights: | Category | What You’re Entitled To | How It Helps | |----------|------------------------|--------------| | **Security Deposit** | • Landlord may charge up to one month’s rent (or two if the lease is for a furnished unit).
• Must return deposit within 30 days after you move out, minus any lawful deductions. | Ensures you get most of your money back if no damage or unpaid rent. | | **Habitability** | • Landlord must keep the property safe, clean, and in good repair (plumbing, heating, electrical, etc.).
• Must fix major problems within a reasonable time after notice. | Guarantees a livable environment. | | **Right to Quiet Enjoyment** | • Landlord cannot enter without proper notice (usually 24 hours) unless it’s an emergency.
• Must respect your privacy. | Protects against unwanted intrusions. | | **Notice Requirements** | • For non‑payment of rent: 3‑day written notice before eviction.
• For lease termination: 30‑day notice for month‑to‑month leases; 60‑day for longer leases. | Gives you time to respond or find new housing. | | **Discrimination Protections** | • Landlords cannot discriminate based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, familial status, or source of income (e.g., public assistance). | Promotes fair treatment. | | **Repair & Deduct / Rent Withhold** | • If landlord fails to fix major issues, you may repair them yourself and deduct costs from rent, or withhold rent until repairs are made.
• Must follow proper procedures (written notice, receipts, etc.). | Allows you to enforce habitability standards. | | **Lease Terms** | • Lease must be in writing if it lasts longer than one year.
• Must include essential terms (rent amount, due date, security deposit, etc.). | Provides clarity and enforceability. | | **Eviction Process** | • Landlord must file a lawsuit and obtain a court order before evicting.
• You have the right to contest the eviction in court. | Prevents unlawful “self‑help” evictions. | ### Practical Tips 1. **Document Everything** – Keep copies of all communications, receipts, and photos of any damage or maintenance requests. 2. **Know Your Lease** – Read it carefully; any clause that conflicts with Texas law is void. 3. **Use Written Notices** – Send notices via certified mail or email with read receipt to prove delivery. 4. **Seek Legal Aid** – If disputes arise, consider contacting a local tenant‑rights organization or a lawyer who specializes in landlord‑tenant law. If you need more detailed guidance—such as how to draft a notice or what to do if your landlord refuses to make repairs—just let me know!
